items.label: section_header
items.text: FINDING THE n IN BaClnH_2O

items.label: section_header
items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: Remember that when some substances crystallise from solution, water becomes chemically bound up with the salt. This is called water of crystallisation. The salt is said to be hydrated.

items.label: section_header
items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: Anhydrous means without water.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 5.15 Heating barium chloride crystals in a crucible

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Barium chloride is toxic but a Bunsen flame is not hot enough to release it into the atmosphere.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: If you are doing this experiment, how can you be sure that all the water has been driven off? The best way to do this is to heat it to constant mass. You heat the crucible and weigh it. Keep doing this until the mass remains constant. If the mass has gone down after heating there may still be water present, but when the mass remains constant after heating you know that all the water has been driven off.

items.label: section_header
items.text: INTERPRETING SYMBOLS IN EQUATIONS IN TERMS OF MOLES

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: The big numbers in front of the formulae tell us the number of moles of each substance that react. Although there does not appear to be a big number in front of the CH4 and CO{2, there should actually be a '1' in front of each but we just don't write it.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EMPIRICAL FORMULA CALCULATIONS INVOLVING WATER OF CRYSTALLISATION

items.label: text
items.text: Usually, when you heat a salt that contains water of crystallisation, the water is driven off, leaving the anhydrous salt behind. Hydrated barium chloride is a commonly used example because the barium chloride itself doesn't decompose even on quite strong heating.

items.label: text
items.text: If you heated barium chloride crystals in a crucible you might obtain these results:

items.label: text
items.text: Mass of crucible =30.00g

items.label: text
items.text: Mass of crucible + barium chloride crystals, BaCl2·n H2O =32.44g

items.label: text
items.text: Mass of crucible + anhydrous barium chloride, BaCl2 = 32.08g

items.label: text
items.text: To find n, you need to find the ratio of the number of moles of BaCl2 to the number of moles of water. It's just another empirical formula calculation (A, of H = 1, A, of O = 16, A, of Cl = 35.5, A, of Ba = 137).

items.label: text
items.text: Mass of water = 32.44 - 32.08 = 0.36g

items.label: table
items.text:
Table 5.2 Finding the n in BaCl2-nH2O0

|                                          | BaCl2      | H2O        |
|------------------------------------------|------------|------------|
| masses/g                                 | 2.08       | 0.36       |
| divide by M, to find the number of moles | 2.08/208   | 0.36/18    |
| number of moles                          | 0.0100     | 0.020      |
| ratio of moles                           | 1          | 2          |
| empirical formula                        | BaCl2.2H2O | BaCl2.2H2O |

items.label: section_header
items.text: CALCULATIONS USING MOLES, CHEMICAL EQUATIONS AND MASSES OF SUBSTANCES CALCULATIONS USING MOLES, CHEMICAL EQUATIONS AND MASSES OF SUBSTANCES

items.label: text
items.text: If we write a chemical equation:

items.label: formula
items.text: C H _ { 4 } + 2 O _ { 2 } \rightarrow C O _ { 2 } + 2 H _ { 2 } O

items.label: text
items.text: we can say that 1 molecule of CH4 combines with 2 molecules of O2 to form 1 molecule of CO2 and 2 molecules of water. When doing calculations, however, it is often more useful to think about this in terms of moles and take symbols as meaning moles of each substance. So here we can say:

items.label: text
items.text: 1 mol CH4 reacts with 2 mol O2 to form 1 mol CO2 and 2 mol H2O

items.label: text
items.text: We have not changed the meaning of the equation as the ratios are still the same.
